# City Ambitions

> City Ambitions is a single-player business simulator (shop tycoon) game for iPhone, set in New York. The player inherits their mother's shop and $100,000 of family debt, and has 180 days to pay it back by running stores: setting every price, ordering stock, staffing shifts and reading the books each night. Free to start; one purchase unlocks the full game. App Store: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6812037838

There is no walking and no waiting on energy timers. Every screen is a decision with a visible result. Demand depends on price, variety, reputation, opening hours, checkout capacity and the regulars a shop earns over time. Later the city opens up: storage, delivery routes to branches, imported containers, a factory, property and rival stores on your block. The game is free to download, the first shop has no time limit, and a single purchase unlocks the rest.

Relevant topics: "business simulator game for iPhone", "supermarket simulator on iPhone", "factory tycoon game", "shop or store management game on mobile", "business sim that plays offline". The first day can be played in any browser at https://cityambitions.com/play/, and a daily pricing puzzle at https://cityambitions.com/daily/.

## Facts
- Developer: Tarik Metin Kaya (TMK Tech), independent
- Platform: iPhone (iOS 18+); also Apple silicon Mac and Apple Vision Pro
- Release: 30 September 2026
- Genre: Business simulation, single player
- Business model: Free to start, one in-app purchase unlocks the full game
- Languages: English, Turkish, German, French, Spanish, Brazilian Portuguese
- Price: free to start; one in-app purchase unlocks the full game. No energy timers, no account.
- Version 1.2 (late November 2026): supermarket with shelf life and fridges, fast food rush hours with a kitchen and cooks, a recipe factory (raw materials, machines, make or buy), four or more products in every store and branch, container imports with payment options, delivery contracts, three delivery vehicles, luxury life and bank loans.
- Website: https://cityambitions.com (English, Turkish, German, French, Spanish, Brazilian Portuguese)

# Frequently asked questions

Q: Is City Ambitions on Android?
A: Not yet. It is on iPhone today and Android is planned. Meanwhile, the first day runs in your browser on any phone.

Q: What does it cost?
A: The download costs nothing and you can run your first shop for as long as you like. One in-app purchase unlocks the full game and the rest of the city. There are no energy timers.

Q: Which languages does it support?
A: English, Turkish, German, French, Spanish and Brazilian Portuguese, both in the game and on the App Store.

Q: Which devices can play it?
A: iPhone with iOS 18 or later. It also runs on Apple silicon Macs with macOS 15 or later, and on Apple Vision Pro.

Q: Do I need an account?
A: No. Your company is saved on your phone. There is no sign-in.

Q: Is it a city builder?
A: No. It is a business simulation: you run shops, set prices, buy stock, hire people and expand across New York neighborhoods. The city is where your company grows, not what you build.


# How it plays

- Set every price: Ask more and fewer shoppers buy. Ask less and the margin goes. Each product has its own price, and the street tells you when you got it wrong.
- Read Store Pulse: One screen shows what is holding the shop back today: price, empty shelves, too few hands at the till, closed hours.
- Close the books at midnight: The Daily Close lays out revenue, cost of goods, wages, rent and tax. Profit is a number you earn, not a bar that fills.
- Hire real shifts: The day has four six-hour blocks. Each hire covers one. Wages, morale and raises are all yours to manage.
- Import by the container: Pick a source, a box size and how to pay. A cheaper unit cost is worth waiting for, until customs holds the ship.
- Grow across the city: Open branches in new neighborhoods, run delivery routes, build a factory, buy property, and keep an eye on rivals on your block.


# Guide: Getting started: your first week
https://cityambitions.com/guides/getting-started/

The opening is short, but three decisions in it follow you for the whole game. Here is what they are and how to make them.
## The goal

Your mother's shop owes $100,000, and you have 180 days to pay it back. You start with $2,000. The company does not end on Day 180: clear the debt and keep building. See how to clear the debt in 180 days.

## Day 1: umbrellas in the rain

You have no store yet. Raymond Cole, a wholesaler, sells umbrellas at cost, and it is raining. You make two choices:

  - How many to buy: 10 to 100, at $4.00 each ($3.80 with Bargaining).

  - What to charge: anything from $5 to $30. The street expects about $12.

Then the rain lasts 30 seconds. Shoppers walk past one by one, each with a price they will not go above. A retired neighbor stops at about $10; a family of four will pay a lot more to stay dry. Anyone who finds your price too high keeps walking.

Tip: the market price is a reference, not a ceiling. In the rain, plenty of people pay well above $12. Push the price up and watch who walks; the result screen shows exactly what it cost you. You can try it in the browser demo first.

One umbrella always stays in your bag. Unsold umbrellas are still yours: they are stock, not a loss, and you can sell them the next day.

## Pick a skill that fits how you play

  Skill | What it does, for the whole game | 

  
    Bargaining | 5% off every supplier order. | 

    Selling | Shoppers accept prices 10% above market before they start walking away. | 

    Numbers | 5% off rent on every store. | 

  

Selling suits players who like to price high. Bargaining pays off most once you buy in volume. Numbers is steady and grows with every store you rent.

## Day 2: your first store

You lease a storefront in the Garment District: an $800 deposit that you get back when you leave, and $60 a day in rent ($57 with Numbers). Then you choose what to sell:

  Product | Unit cost | Market price | 

  
    Silk scarf | $8 | $22 | 

    Basic t-shirt | $7 | $20 | 

    Denim jacket | $24 | $65 | 

  

Scarves and t-shirts sell faster. Jackets sell slowly at a fat margin. You hire two people: one covers the afternoon block, the other the evening.

## The first week

A coach walks you through the shop one lesson at a time: setting a price, ordering stock, speeding up the clock and opening more hours. Every night at midnight the Daily Close shows revenue, cost of goods, wages, rent and tax. Read it every day; it is the fastest way to learn what worked.

## Mistakes that cost the most early

  - Running the shelf empty. Shoppers who find nothing to buy leave, and regulars drift away. Order before you run out; local wholesale orders arrive the next morning.

  - Pricing far below market. It brings people in, but if your staff cannot serve them all you are giving margin away. See how pricing works.

  - Ignoring Store Pulse. It names the one thing holding the shop back today. See regulars and Store Pulse.

## After the first shop

You can run your first shop for as long as you like. The Full Game, a single purchase, opens the rest of the city: more storefronts, storage, containers, your own factory, buildings, deposits and shares.


# Guide: Factory tycoon game on iPhone: make it yourself or buy it wholesale
https://cityambitions.com/guides/factory-tycoon-game-iphone/

Most factory games are about conveyor belts. In City Ambitions the factory is a business decision: is it cheaper to make this product yourself, or to keep buying it wholesale?
## How the factory works

From version 1.2, City Ambitions' factory runs on recipes. Each recipe turns raw materials into a product on a machine, with workers on the floor. You buy the raw materials from a wholesaler or import them by container, the machines produce every morning, and the goods go straight to your stores' storage.

A silk scarf line: 240 a morning, make for $3.49 or buy for $8.

## The make-or-buy decision

The factory screen shows, for every product, what it costs to make and what it costs to buy. That gap is the whole game:

  - Make it when the gap is large and your stores sell enough to keep the line busy.

  - Buy it when demand is small or uneven: an idle line still costs rent and wages.

  - Sell the surplus wholesale when the factory makes more than your stores can sell.

## Getting started

  - Grow one or two stores until you know what sells every day.

  - Start with a small floor and one recipe for your best-selling product.

  - Keep raw materials stocked: an empty input stops the line.

  - Add machines and workers only when the line is full every morning.

  - Compare the factory's cost per unit with your old wholesale price in the Daily Close.

## The rest of the company

The factory is one part of a bigger business sim: shops, supermarkets and fast food in New York neighborhoods, branches with delivery routes and three kinds of vehicle, container imports, delivery contracts, bank loans and, when you are rich, a luxury life. See how to run a store in a business sim for the basics, and the best business sim games on iPhone for other options.


# Guide: How to clear $100,000 of debt in 180 days in City Ambitions
https://cityambitions.com/guides/clear-100000-debt-in-180-days/

Your mother's shop owes $100,000 and the bank wants it in 180 days. The good news: the game does not ask for $100,000 in cash. Here is what it measures, and a plan to get there.
## What the game checks on Day 180

When Day 180 closes, City Ambitions compares your company value with the $100,000 debt. Company value is everything the company owns, minus what it still owes:

  - Counts: cash, stock on shelves and in storage (at cost), branches (part of what you spent setting them up), buildings you own, deposits, shares.

  - Comes off: container orders not yet paid for, and what you still owe the bank on a loan.

  - Does not count: money spent on the luxury life. It is spending, and the cash is gone.

There are three endings, and none of them is game over:

  Company value on Day 180 | What happens | 

  
    $100,000 or more | The debt is paid. The shop is your mother's again. | 

    $60,000 to $99,999 | Short, but close: the bank takes the rest in instalments and the doors stay open. | 

    Below $60,000 | The shop goes back to the bank. Everything else you built is still yours, and you keep playing. | 

  

The Home screen shows your progress against the debt every day, so you always know where you stand.

## Days 1 to 7: learn one shop properly

You start with $2,000 and one storefront. The first week is not about money; it is about learning what your shop's numbers mean.

  - Sell out your umbrellas on Day 1 at a price above market: the rain makes people pay. See getting started.

  - Never let the shelf run empty. Shoppers who find nothing leave, and regulars stop coming.

  - Read the Daily Close every night. Revenue minus cost of goods, wages, rent and tax is your real profit.

## Days 8 to 40: make the first shop boring

A shop that runs itself is the base you build on. Aim for a full shelf, a price near the top of what shoppers accept, and staff on the busy blocks.

  - Price up until profit stops rising. Change one price at a time and compare the next close. See how pricing works.

  - Open the hours that pay. A block with few shoppers can cost more in wages than it earns. See staff and opening hours.

  - Earn regulars. They come back every day without being won over again. See regulars and Store Pulse.

## Days 40 to 120: grow the value, not only the cash

This is where most of the $100,000 comes from. Profit that sits in the bank counts, but so does profit you turn into things the company owns.

  - Open a second store in another neighborhood once the first one is full every day. Each branch adds its own daily profit.

  - Cut your unit cost. Storage and container imports lower what each product costs you; the saving is profit on every sale. See stock, storage and containers.

  - Try a supermarket or fast food (version 1.2) when you can staff it. More shoppers, smaller margins.

  - Consider a factory for a product you sell in volume. See the factory guide.

## Days 120 to 180: protect what you have

  - Watch the progress bar, not the cash. A big container order lowers company value until it is paid and landed; time large orders so they arrive and sell before Day 180.

  - Hold off on the luxury life until the debt is covered. A watch or a yacht is a reward, not an investment.

  - Use a bank loan for growth only. The loan's cash counts and what you owe comes off, so a loan only helps if the business you build with it earns more than the interest.

## Mistakes that leave you short

  - Expanding before the first shop is profitable: two weak stores lose money twice as fast.

  - Pricing far below market to look busy when staff cannot serve the crowd.

  - Over-ordering perishable goods in a supermarket: spoiled stock is money thrown away.

  - Spending on luxury before Day 180.

Questions

### Do I need $100,000 in cash on Day 180?

No. City Ambitions measures company value: cash plus stock, branches, buildings, deposits and shares, minus unpaid orders and loans. Luxury purchases do not count.

### What happens if I do not clear the debt?

Above 60% of the debt, the bank takes the rest in instalments and the shop stays open. Below that, the shop goes back to the bank, but the rest of your company is still yours and the game goes on.

### Does the game end on Day 180?

No. The deadline settles the debt once, and then you keep playing with no time limit.

### Can I try the start before downloading?

Yes: the first day plays in your browser.


# Guide: Business sim economy guide: pricing, stock and staff, explained with real numbers
https://cityambitions.com/guides/business-sim-economy-guide/

Every business sim runs on the same few equations: how many shoppers come, how many you can serve, what each sale earns, and what the day costs. Understand those and any shop makes sense.
## The one equation: daily profit

Daily profit = units sold × (price − unit cost) − wages − rent − tax. Every decision in a business sim moves one of those terms:

  Lever | What it moves | The catch | 

  
    Price | Margin per sale | Fewer shoppers accept a higher price | 

    Stock | How many units can sell | Cash tied up, storage, spoilage | 

    Staff | How many shoppers you can serve | Wages every block you open | 

    Supplier | Unit cost | Minimum orders and delivery time | 

    Location | How many shoppers walk past | Rent | 

  

In City Ambitions the Daily Close at midnight shows each term, so you can see which lever moved.

The Daily Close: every term of the profit equation, every night.

## Demand: who comes, and who buys

Shoppers come from the neighborhood's foot traffic and from your regulars. Each one compares your price with the product's market price. In City Ambitions the share who still buy falls as your price rises above market; the full curve is in how pricing works.

So the best price is rarely the market price. It is the price where units × margin is highest, and that depends on whether you can serve everyone anyway.

## Capacity: the cap nobody sees

Sales are the smallest of three numbers: shoppers who want to buy, units on the shelf, and shoppers your staff can serve. Raising any of the others does nothing while the smallest one holds.

  - Shelf is the limit: order more, or more often.

  - Staff is the limit: hire for the busy block, or raise the price so the shoppers you serve pay more.

  - Demand is the limit: lower the price a little, open better hours, or earn regulars.

Staff decide how many shoppers a block can serve.

## Unit cost: the lever that scales

A lower unit cost raises profit on every sale in every store. In City Ambitions the path is local wholesale, then storage and bulk orders, then container imports (pay up front, by letter of credit or on landing), then a factory that makes the product from raw materials. Each step cuts the cost but ties up more cash for longer. See stock, storage and containers.

Margin is price minus unit cost; containers and factories move the cost side.

## Fixed costs: rent and wages

Rent is paid whether you sell or not, and a staffed block costs wages even when it is quiet. That is why a second store only pays once the first one is profitable, and why closing a dead block can raise profit without a single extra sale.

## Cash versus value

Profit is not the same as cash. Stock you bought is still worth its cost; a container in transit is cash already spent. City Ambitions' goal is measured in company value, not cash, which changes how you plan the last weeks. See how to clear $100,000 of debt in 180 days.

Questions

### Should I price at the market price?

Start there, then raise it step by step. If your staff cannot serve everyone, a higher price earns more from the same shoppers.

### Why is my shop busy but not profitable?

Usually staff or shelf is the limit, or wages for quiet blocks eat the margin. Check which number is smallest: demand, stock or service.

### When should I open a second store?

When the first one is full every day and profitable after rent and wages. A second weak store doubles the losses.

### Where can I practise this?

The daily pricing puzzle and the browser demo both run on City Ambitions' real numbers.


# Guide: How pricing works
https://cityambitions.com/guides/pricing/

Every product has a market price: what shoppers on that block expect to pay. Where you set yours against it decides how many of them buy.
## The range

You can price any product from half its market price up to double it, in whole dollars. A $22 silk scarf can sell for anything from $11 to $44.

## The price curve

The game reads your price as a percentage of the market price and turns it into price appeal: how strongly the block is drawn to your shelf compared with a shelf priced at market. These are the numbers it uses:

  Your price vs market | Price appeal | 

  
    60% or less | 160% | 

    61% to 80% | 130% | 

    81% to 100% | 100% | 

    110% | 86% | 

    120% | 71% | 

    130% | 56% | 

    150% | 40% | 

    180% | 16% | 

    above 180% | 10% | 

  

Three things stand out:

  - Up to market price, nothing is lost. Anything from 81% to 100% reads the same, so pricing at 85% of market gives away margin for no extra shoppers.

  - Discounts work in steps. You only gain shoppers at 80% of market or below, and again at 60%.

  - Above market, appeal falls steadily: about 1.5 points for every percent up to 130%, then more slowly.

Selling skill: if you chose Selling in the opening, the game treats every market price as 10% higher. Your whole curve shifts right: a price 10% above market reads like market price.

## Margin against volume: a worked example

A denim jacket costs $24 and the market price is $65.

  Price | Margin per jacket | Appeal | Margin × appeal | 

  
    $55 | $31 | 100% | 31 | 

    $65 | $41 | 100% | 41 | 

    $70 | $46 | 90% | 41 | 

    $78 | $54 | 71% | 38 | 

  

When you can serve everyone who wants to buy, market price or a little above earns the most per shopper. Going far above loses more buyers than the margin wins back.

## When to raise prices anyway

The curve above assumes every interested shopper gets served. Often they cannot be. If the Daily Close says shoppers gave up in the queue, or Store Pulse points at checkout capacity, your staff are the limit, not your price. Those shoppers are lost either way, so a higher price that sends some of them away costs you nothing and earns more on everyone you do serve. Raise the price until the queue clears, or hire for another block.

## Other things that move demand

  - Variety. A shop with more lines stocked draws more people: two lines bring 8% more footfall, three 14%, four 18%.

  - Regulars. Served well, some shoppers come back on their own. See regulars and Store Pulse.

  - Opening hours. A block with nobody working sells nothing. See staff and opening hours.

  - The city. Weekdays, events, trends and rivals on your block all move the crowd. Store Pulse and the City tab show them.

## How to tell if the price is wrong

Shoppers who find the price too high show up in the store's customer feed and in Store Pulse. A few are normal when you price above market. If they are most of your feed, step the price down a dollar or two and compare the next Daily Close.


# Guide: Regulars and Store Pulse
https://cityambitions.com/guides/regulars-and-store-pulse/

Store Pulse answers one question: what is holding this shop back today? Regulars are the one part of demand you build yourself.
## The sentence at the top

Store Pulse opens with one line, for example: "About 120 shoppers come in today, 18 of them regulars, wanting 150 items." It then names the limit that bites first:

  - The shelf is empty. Order stock in Supply.

  - Stock runs out first. You have fewer items than people want. Order more, or rent storage once it opens.

  - The line is the limit. Your staff cannot serve everyone. Hire for another block, raise the price, or both (see pricing).

  - You can serve every one of them. The shop is healthy. Grow demand: promotion, more lines, more hours.

## The factors

  Factor | What it means | 

  
    Basket | How much an average shopper carries out. One product on the shelf means one thing per shopper. Several lines in real depth and the same shoppers spend more. | 

    Location traffic | How busy the block is. It is the base for promotion. | 

    Promotion | How many of the block's shoppers know your store. Campaigns raise it above location traffic, up to 100%. | 

    Open hours | Shoppers only come while the doors are open. Afternoons and evenings bring 70% of a day's shoppers, mornings 20%, nights 10%. | 

    Reputation | Recent reviews as a demand multiplier. Three and a half stars is neutral; a five-star shop pulls about three times the crowd of a one-star shop. | 

    Staff skill | Average sales skill of today's staff, with their morale. | 

    Product trend | Where your main product sits in its cycle: rising, peak, saturation or dead stock. | 

    Rivals | The share of walk-ins your store keeps when rivals open on the same block. | 

  

The day of the week matters too. The busiest day brings about 1.7 times the shoppers of the quietest, so a slow day is not always a problem to fix.

## How regulars work

Regulars are people who count your shop as theirs. They walk in again without any marketing behind them, and they are what makes Day 100 feel different from Day 3.

  - Winning them: every night, about 1 in 9 shoppers who were served properly becomes a regular.

  - Visits: each regular drops in on roughly 1 day in 5.

  - Losing them: regulars drift away by about 2% a day even when nothing goes wrong. Every percent of the day's shoppers you turn away (empty shelf, long line, closed door) adds to that drift.

  - A bad day wins nobody: if more than half of the day's shoppers leave unserved, no one new becomes a regular that night.

  - A ceiling: a block only holds so many people who could adopt one shop, so regulars level off over time.

The lesson: an empty shelf costs more than today's lost sales. It thins out the regulars you spent weeks building. Keep stock and staff ahead of demand, especially in the first month.

## A checklist when sales stall

  - Read the Store Pulse sentence. Is it stock, the line, or demand?

  - Check the shopper feed for "found the price too high". If it dominates, step the price down.

  - Count staffed blocks. Two of four blocks means the doors are closed for 30% of shoppers.

  - Look at Product trend. A cooling product needs a new line beside it.

  - Compare tomorrow's Daily Close. Change one thing at a time so you can tell what worked.


# Guide: Stock, storage and containers
https://cityambitions.com/guides/stock-and-storage/

Running out costs you sales and regulars. Overbuying ties up cash in boxes. This guide covers how much to hold and where to keep it.
## Ordering

Orders from a local wholesaler arrive the next morning. Other suppliers and containers take longer. Store Pulse tells you every day how many items shoppers want; if that number is larger than what is on the shelf, stock runs out first.

A good habit: after the Daily Close, look at what sold today and make sure tomorrow's shelf can cover at least that, plus a margin for the busier days of the week.

Unsold stock is not a loss. It stays on the books at what you paid for it and counts toward your net worth. The cost of goods only hits your profit when something sells.

## The shelf

Your first store's shelf holds 120 units. Shelving upgrades add more. Anything you order beyond the shelf needs storage.

## Storage

Storage holds overflow stock and refills the shelf every morning. It opens (with the Full Game) on any of three roads, and never during the first week:

  - three closes lost to an empty shelf,

  - every shelving upgrade already bought, or

  - a day whose demand is at least half the shelf.

  Unit | Holds | Rent per day | 

  
    Small unit | 400 | $60 | 

    Large unit | 1,200 | $200 | 

  

Rent is charged at every close, full or empty, so rent the small unit first. The large one is sized for containers.

## Containers

Importing by container cuts the unit cost of a product, often by a lot. In return you wait days for the ship, pay for many units at once, and accept that customs, strikes and damage can change what arrives and when.

The importer only offers once your company moves an average of 45 units a day over the last week. A container is 300 units, so that makes it about a week of sales: worth the wait, without leaving money sitting in a room for a month.

When you order, you choose:

  - the source: cheaper sources take longer and carry more risk,

  - the box size: bigger boxes are cheaper per unit but must fit in your storage,

  - how to pay: paying up front is cheapest, paying on landing keeps cash in the shop for longer.

When the ship lands and the new stock lowers your average unit cost, the game shows a Margin Win: what each unit cost before and after, and how much more you now make on every sale at the same price.

## Branches and delivery routes

Once you run more than one storefront, a van and driver can carry stock from your storage to the branches each morning, up to the van's capacity and the driver's number of stops. A branch's unit cost blends in the cost of what the route brings.


# Guide: Staff and opening hours
https://cityambitions.com/guides/staff-and-opening-hours/

Your doors are only open while someone is working, and each person can only serve so many shoppers. Staffing decides both.
## Four blocks a day

The day is split into four six-hour blocks. Each hire covers one block, every day of the week. Shoppers arrive unevenly across them:

  Block | Hours | Share of the day's shoppers | 

  
    Morning | 6 AM – 12 PM | 20% | 

    Afternoon | 12 – 6 PM | 35% | 

    Evening | 6 PM – 12 AM | 35% | 

    Night | 12 – 6 AM | 10% | 

  

Your first two hires take the afternoon and the evening, which already covers 70% of shoppers. A morning hire adds the next 20%; a night hire is worth it only once everything else is full.

## How many shoppers one person serves

One person looks after about 26 shoppers per six-hour block at 80% sales skill, which is roughly four an hour once greeting, fitting and the till are counted. Higher skill serves more, lower skill fewer, and morale scales it too.

When more people want to buy than your staff can handle, the extra shoppers leave after seeing the line. The Daily Close counts them, and Store Pulse says "the line is the limit".

Two fixes for a long line: hire for another block, or raise the price. A higher price sends away some of the people who were going to leave anyway, and earns more on everyone you serve. See how pricing works.

## Wages and morale

Every person has a wage, a sales skill and a morale. Morale starts at 80%. Unhappy staff sell less, may ask for a raise, and a person who stays unhappy for a week can resign. Watch the Staff page for raise requests and answer them before they turn into resignations.

## Opening hours and regulars

A closed block does more than lose that block's sales: shoppers who could not get in count as turned away, and turning people away is what makes regulars drift off. See regulars and Store Pulse.

## Autopilot

Later in the game you can hire a manager. Only businesses covered by Executive Autopilot keep running while you are away from the game.


# Guide: The best business sim games on iPhone (2026)
https://cityambitions.com/guides/business-sim-games-iphone/

Looking for a real business simulator on your phone? Here is what is out there in 2026, what each game is actually about, and how to choose.
Full disclosure: we make City Ambitions, the first game on this list. Every other game here is made by someone else and is listed because it is worth knowing about.

## What makes a good business sim (and not just an idle clicker)

Many games in the App Store's tycoon section are idle games: numbers go up while you wait, and the main decision is which upgrade to tap. A business simulator is different. Look for:

  - Prices you set yourself, with demand that reacts to them.

  - Costs that can sink you: rent, wages, stock that does not sell.

  - Staff and opening hours that limit how much you can sell.

  - A way to grow: more stores, better suppliers, your own production.

  - Few or no timers and ads standing between you and your next decision.

## The list

### 1. City Ambitions: a deep shop-and-company sim for iPhone

A single-player business simulator set in New York. You inherit your mother's shop and $100,000 of family debt, and you have 180 days to clear it. You set every price, order every box, staff four six-hour shifts and read a full profit and loss every night. Later you open branches in other neighborhoods, rent storage, run delivery routes, import containers, build a factory and face rival stores on your block.

  - Best for: players who want real numbers and real decisions on a phone.

  - Model: free to start; one purchase unlocks the full game. No energy timers.

  - Platforms: iPhone (also Apple silicon Mac and Apple Vision Pro). Not on Android yet.

  - Try it: play the first day in your browser, or get it on the App Store.

### 2. Sim Companies: an online economy with other players

A multiplayer business game where you build production chains and trade on a market made of other real players. Prices come from them, not from a script. It is closer to an economic strategy game than to running a single shop, and it rewards patience over weeks.

  - Best for: players who like markets, supply chains and competing with real people.

  - Platforms: iPhone, Android and web.

### 3. Game Dev Tycoon: run a game studio

You start in a garage making games and grow into a studio, choosing topics, genres and platforms and reading reviews of what you ship. A small, focused management game with a clear goal and a strong sense of progress.

  - Best for: players who want a contained story of building a company from nothing.

  - Platforms: iPhone, Android and PC.

### 4. Good Pizza, Great Pizza: a small shop, one customer at a time

A pizza shop where you read each customer's order, make the pizza and earn enough to buy better equipment. Lighter than a full business sim, but it captures the feeling of running a shop day by day.

  - Best for: short, relaxed sessions with a shop at the center.

  - Platforms: iPhone, Android and PC.

### 5. Business Inc. and Business Empire: big-company fantasies

Both are popular tycoon games about growing a fortune across many kinds of businesses. They lean toward the empire-building fantasy and fast progress rather than the details of one store's pricing and staffing.

  - Best for: players who want scale and quick growth.

  - Platforms: iPhone and Android.

### 6. Founder Sim: a startup instead of a shop

A newer iPhone game (2026) about founding and running a startup. If your interest is the company side, such as hiring, funding and product, rather than retail, it is worth a look.

  - Platforms: iPhone.

## How to choose

  If you want... | Try |

    A real player-driven market | Sim Companies | 

    A compact company story | Game Dev Tycoon | 

    A light, cozy shop | Good Pizza, Great Pizza | 

    Fast empire-building | Business Inc., Business Empire |

# Guide: Supermarket simulator on iPhone: run a grocery store that can spoil
https://cityambitions.com/guides/supermarket-simulator-iphone/

A good supermarket sim is not about scanning barcodes. It is about the decisions a grocer makes: what to stock, how much, at what price, and what to do before the milk goes off.
## What makes a supermarket different from a shop

A clothing store sells a few things at a fat margin. A supermarket sells many cheap things to many people. That changes how you play:

  - Volume over margin. Each item earns little, so footfall and basket size matter more than any single price.

  - Food spoils. Milk, bread and fruit only last a few days. Order too much and you throw money away at closing.

  - Cold storage is a limit. Fresh goods need fridge space, so the fridges cap how much you can keep.

  - The checkout is the bottleneck. Big baskets take longer to ring up, so staff and registers decide how many shoppers you can serve.

A supermarket in Murray Hill, version 1.2.

## The supermarket in City Ambitions

From version 1.2 you can open a supermarket as one of your businesses in New York. It sells everyday groceries, from milk and eggs to bread, fruit, pasta, cereal and frozen pizza. Every product has its own price, and the Daily Close shows what sold, what it cost and, new for groceries, what spoiled.

A supermarket pulls far more shoppers than a boutique (the one in the screenshot serves 345 a day), but each sale is small. The skill is keeping the shelves full of what moves without over-ordering what rots.

## Tips for running a grocery store well

  - Order fresh goods little and often. A short shelf life punishes big orders. Let longer-lasting lines carry the big orders instead.

  - Price staples close to market. In a high-volume store a small discount on a basic can bring a lot of extra baskets; check the next Daily Close before you go further.

  - Watch the spoiled line. If the same product spoils every few days, order less of it or price it to move.

  - Staff for the crowd. If shoppers give up in the queue, hire for another block before you cut prices. See staff and opening hours.

  - Use delivery contracts. A supplier can top up your shelves every morning so you never forget an order.

## Is it a real simulator or an idle game?

City Ambitions has no timers to wait on and no automatic money. Demand comes from your prices, stock, staff, opening hours and the regulars you earn, so a badly run supermarket loses money. If you want the full picture of how demand works, read how pricing works and regulars and Store Pulse.

## Other business sims on iPhone

If you want a wider view, our list of the best business sim games on iPhone compares several, and how to run a store in a business sim covers the basics that apply to every shop.


# Guide: Offline business tycoon games for iPhone, and how to spot the ad-heavy ones
https://cityambitions.com/guides/offline-business-tycoon-games-iphone/

Plenty of tycoon games need a connection to show you ads, sync timers or check a server. Here is how to find business games that play anywhere, and how to read an App Store page before you download.
## What "offline" really means for a mobile game

A game plays offline when everything you do is calculated and saved on your phone. Signs that it does:

  - No account or sign-in to start playing.

  - Saves on the device, not "in the cloud only".

  - No server-driven events that need you online at a certain hour.

Buying, restoring a purchase or downloading an update always needs a connection, on any game.

## How to spot an ad-heavy tycoon game before you install it

Many games in the App Store's tycoon section are idle games: numbers go up on their own, and the main way to go faster is to watch an ad. They can be fun, but they are a different kind of game. Clues on the App Store page:

  - Screenshots showing "x2" or "watch to boost" buttons.

  - Energy, stamina or "come back in 4 hours" timers.

  - A long list of small in-app purchases (gem packs, coin bundles) instead of a single unlock.

  - Reviews mentioning ads after every action.

A business simulator, by contrast, makes you decide prices, stock and staff, and a bad decision costs you money.

The Daily Close: the books close at midnight, on your phone.

## City Ambitions

City Ambitions is a single-player business simulator set in New York. Your company is saved on your iPhone, there is no account, and the simulation runs on the device, so you can play without a connection once it is installed. There are no energy timers and no automatic money: you set prices, order stock, staff shifts and read a full profit and loss every night, then expand into supermarkets, fast food, branches, containers and your own factory.

Price: free to start; one in-app purchase unlocks the full game. Check the App Store page for the current details.

# Guide: How to run a store in a business sim: pricing, stock and staff tips
https://cityambitions.com/guides/how-to-run-a-store-business-sim/

Every shop in a business sim comes down to three questions: what to charge, how much to keep on the shelf, and how many people you need at the till. Get those right and the rest is growth.
## 1. Pricing: start at market, then listen

Most business sims give each product a market price: what shoppers expect to pay. Start there. Raise the price a little and watch two things: how many shoppers walk away, and whether profit per day goes up.

  - Pricing below market rarely pays unless you are clearing stock or your store has spare capacity.

  - Pricing above market works when you cannot serve everyone anyway: the shoppers you lose were going to leave the queue.

  - Change one price at a time and compare the next day's results.

Every product has its own price slider and market price.
In City Ambitions the numbers behind this are public: see how pricing works for the exact price curve.

## 2. Stock: never run the shelf empty

An empty shelf loses today's sale and, in most sims, tomorrow's customer. A full warehouse ties up cash. Aim in between:

  - Keep at least one day of sales on the shelf, plus a margin for busy days.

  - Order before you run out, not after: deliveries take time.

  - Buy in bulk only when the unit cost drops enough to pay for the storage.

  - For perishable goods, order little and often.

More detail: stock, storage and containers.

## 3. Staff: the hidden cap on sales

Customers who cannot be served leave. If your shop is busy but profit is flat, the till is probably the limit.

  - Staff the busiest hours first; nights and early mornings usually come last.

  - Watch morale and raise requests before people quit.

  - When the queue is the limit, a higher price can earn more than another hire.

Four six-hour blocks a day; each hire covers one.
More detail: staff and opening hours.

## 4. Read the books every day

The daily report is the best teacher in any business sim. Revenue, cost of goods, wages, rent and tax tell you which decision worked. In City Ambitions this is the Daily Close at midnight.

## 5. Grow when one store is boring

When a store runs itself, open the next one: a new neighborhood, a new kind of business (a supermarket or fast food from version 1.2), a container import to lower costs, or a factory to make your own goods.

## Try it

You can practise pricing and stock in City Ambitions' first day in your browser, or try the daily pricing puzzle. For the numbers behind it, read the business sim economy guide. For other games, see the best business sim games on iPhone.
